results.name: cell_response_graded_ness_multi
results.description: Over (set, target) cells from sets of 2+ examples, the mean of p*(1-p) where p is the cell's yes-rate across its repeated responses; observed < model means people's answers per item are more consensual/all-or-none than the model's graded posterior-mixture probabilities produce, observed > model means more within-item disagreement than predicted.
results.code:
# name: cell_response_graded_ness_multi
# description: Over (set, target) cells from sets of 2+ examples, the mean of p*(1-p) where p is the cell's yes-rate across its repeated responses; observed < model means people's answers per item are more consensual/all-or-none than the model's graded posterior-mixture probabilities produce, observed > model means more within-item disagreement than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",") + 1
    d = df.loc[n >= 2]
    p = d.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean().to_numpy(dtype=float)
    return float(np.mean(p * (1 - p))) if len(p) else 0.0

results.name: near_rule_violator_yes
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples all divisible by 3, 4, 5 or 10 (or all sharing a last digit), yes-rate on non-example targets within 5 of the nearest example that violate every such shared rule; observed > model means numeric proximity pulls people to "yes" despite a rule violation more than the model predicts, observed < model means people reject nearby rule violators more sharply.
results.code:
# name: near_rule_violator_yes
# description: For sets of 2+ examples all divisible by 3, 4, 5 or 10 (or all sharing a last digit), yes-rate on non-example targets within 5 of the nearest example that violate every such shared rule; observed > model means numeric proximity pulls people to "yes" despite a rule violation more than the model predicts, observed < model means people reject nearby rule violators more sharply.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    tf = t.astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    has_rule = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    satisfies = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for k in (3, 4, 5, 10):
        r = np.all(~valid | (np.mod(ex, k) == 0), axis=1)
        has_rule |= r
        satisfies |= r & (t % k == 0)
    ld = np.mod(ex, 10)
    same = np.nanmax(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmin(ld, axis=1)
    has_rule |= same
    satisfies |= same & (t % 10 == np.mod(ex[:, 0], 10))
    near = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - tf[:, None]), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == tf[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & has_rule & ~satisfies & ~is_ex & (near <= 5)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: interior_yes_mixed_parity_sets
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples with mixed parity (no parity rule) and range >= 15, yes-rate on non-example targets strictly inside the examples' min-max range; observed < model means people fill in the range between scattered examples less than the model's interval concepts predict, observed > model means more.
results.code:
# name: interior_yes_mixed_parity_sets
# description: For sets of 2+ examples with mixed parity (no parity rule) and range >= 15, yes-rate on non-example targets strictly inside the examples' min-max range; observed < model means people fill in the range between scattered examples less than the model's interval concepts predict, observed > model means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.mod(ex, 2)
    mixed = (np.nanmax(par, axis=1) != np.nanmin(par, axis=1))
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & mixed & (hi - lo >= 15) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~is_ex
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: round_target_bias_outside_range
results.description: For targets outside the examples' min-max range, in sets with no example divisible by 10, yes-rate on targets divisible by 10 minus yes-rate on other targets; observed > model means people favour round (decade) numbers as targets more than the model predicts, observed < model means less.
results.code:
# name: round_target_bias_outside_range
# description: For targets outside the examples' min-max range, in sets with no example divisible by 10, yes-rate on targets divisible by 10 minus yes-rate on other targets; observed > model means people favour round (decade) numbers as targets more than the model predicts, observed < model means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    no_round = ~np.any(np.mod(ex, 10) == 0, axis=1)
    out = ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & no_round
    r = out & (t % 10 == 0); o = out & (t % 10 != 0)
    if not r.any() or not o.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[r].mean() - y[o].mean())

results.name: upward_vs_downward_extension
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate on targets 1-20 above the largest example minus yes-rate on targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed > model means people extend the range upward more readily than the model predicts (asymmetric magnitude generalization), observed < model means they extend downward more.
results.code:
# name: upward_vs_downward_extension
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate on targets 1-20 above the largest example minus yes-rate on targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed > model means people extend the range upward more readily than the model predicts (asymmetric magnitude generalization), observed < model means they extend downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    up = (n >= 2) & (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 20)
    dn = (n >= 2) & (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 20)
    if not up.any() or not dn.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[up].mean() - y[dn].mean())

results.name: shared_last_digit_rule_contrast_multi
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes-rate on non-example targets with that last digit minus yes-rate on targets without it; observed > model means people apply the "ends in d" rule more sharply after multiple examples than the model predicts, observed < model means they apply it more weakly (more similarity/range-based).
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_rule_contrast_multi
# description: For sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes-rate on non-example targets with that last digit minus yes-rate on targets without it; observed > model means people apply the "ends in d" rule more sharply after multiple examples than the model predicts, observed < model means they apply it more weakly (more similarity/range-based).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(ex, 10)
    same = np.nanmax(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmin(ld, axis=1)
    d0 = np.mod(ex[:, 0], 10)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & same & ~is_ex
    a = base & (t % 10 == d0); b = base & (t % 10 != d0)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: broad_even_generalization_after_many_even
results.description: Among sets of 3-4 examples that are all even, the yes-rate on even non-example targets; observed > model means people keep generalizing to the broad "even numbers" concept after several examples more than the model's size-principle posterior (which collapses onto narrow rules like powers of 2) predicts, observed < model means they narrow even more sharply.
results.code:
# name: broad_even_generalization_after_many_even
# description: Among sets of 3-4 examples that are all even, the yes-rate on even non-example targets; observed > model means people keep generalizing to the broad "even numbers" concept after several examples more than the model's size-principle posterior (which collapses onto narrow rules like powers of 2) predicts, observed < model means they narrow even more sharply.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    all_even = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (np.mod(ex, 2) == 0), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & all_even & (t % 2 == 0) & ~is_ex
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets within 10 of the first- or last-shown example, yes-rate on targets strictly closer to the last-shown example minus yes-rate on targets strictly closer to the first-shown; observed > model means people generalize more around the most recent example (recency) than the order-blind model predicts, observed < model means a primacy bias.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first_example
# description: For sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets within 10 of the first- or last-shown example, yes-rate on targets strictly closer to the last-shown example minus yes-rate on targets strictly closer to the first-shown; observed > model means people generalize more around the most recent example (recency) than the order-blind model predicts, observed < model means a primacy bias.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    df_ = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex & (np.minimum(df_, dl) <= 10)
    a = base & (dl < df_); b = base & (df_ < dl)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
